Two tables serve this section. Table~\ref{tab:master_abs_codellama7b} is the complete grid for
CodeLlama-7B, the one model on which every arm exists: every condition and stack against every
adaptation, in both directions. Table~\ref{tab:main} is the panel summary: every arm on every model, by condition group, as raw
accuracy and as a percentage of the untuned model's \emph{clean-code} accuracy. The same per-condition detail for the
other seven models is Appendix~\ref{app:absmaster}. We read both against the three questions in turn.

\subsection{RQ1: What Merging Composes}
\label{sec:rq1}
If merging only combined transform-specific adaptations, its advantage would be confined to the
transforms its specialists were trained on, and it would track the union of their individual
competences. It does neither.

On the seen stacks the merge is \emph{not} the strongest arm --- the KL-consistency objective and the
router system are ahead of it by three to six points (Section~\ref{sec:rq2}). If merging were simply
recombining transform-specific surface knowledge, this is where it should win, because these are
exactly the transforms its ingredients were fitted to. It does not. Its advantage appears instead
where the transform surface is unfamiliar: on the held-out family, on stacks containing it, and on
the reverse task, where no arm was trained at all. That pattern is the signature of a general
capability rather than a union of specific ones.

\subsubsection{Adaptation Recovers --- and Exceeds --- Clean-Code Accuracy}
\label{sec:recovery}
The sharpest evidence is what the percentages in Table~\ref{tab:main} are relative to. The reference
is the untuned model's accuracy on \texttt{L0}, unobfuscated source: the performance obfuscation
takes away. Reading the forward half of the table against it, adaptation does not merely claw back
part of that loss.

Untuned, obfuscation costs the panel between 8\,\% and 53\,\% of clean-code accuracy: the untuned
models retain 75--92\,\% of their \texttt{L0} accuracy on single transforms, 61--83\,\% on depth-2
stacks, and 47--63\,\% on the held-out family. After adaptation the same models, still reading
obfuscated programs, reach 132--195\,\% of clean-code accuracy on single transforms, 110--180\,\% on
depth-2 stacks, and 110--174\,\% at depths three and four. Across the merge, KL-consistency and
router arms, \textbf{78 of 84 model\,$\times$\,condition-group cells are at or above 100\,\% of the
untuned model's clean-code accuracy} --- 93\,\%.

This is a stronger statement than ``adaptation helps''. A model fine-tuned on obfuscated code reads
obfuscated programs \emph{better than the original model reads clean ones}. The obfuscation is not
being tolerated; the adaptation is teaching something the model did not have on unobfuscated source
either. It holds even where the transform was never seen: on the held-out family the adapted arms
reach 82--132\,\% of clean-code accuracy, recovering the whole of the obfuscation penalty on six of
the eight models.

The backward direction is the exception, and it is exactly the one the rest of the paper is about.
There only 29 of 78 cells reach 100\,\%, and the merge is the arm that comes closest. Recovery to
clean-code level is a property of the direction that was trained, not of the adaptation as such.

\begin{takeaway}{RQ1}
Merging composes a general program-reasoning capability, not a union of transform-specific ones: it
is not the best arm on the transforms its specialists were built from, and is strongest where the
surface is unfamiliar. More broadly, forward adaptation on obfuscated code does not merely recover
the accuracy obfuscation removes --- it \emph{exceeds} the untuned model's clean-code accuracy on
93\,\% of model\,$\times$\,condition-group cells, including on an obfuscator family no arm ever saw.
That recovery is direction-specific: it does not extend to the untrained direction.
\end{takeaway}

\subsection{RQ2: Composing Capabilities for Stacked Obfuscation}
\label{sec:rq2}
Every strategy works on stacks assembled from seen transforms, and the differences between them are
small. On depth-2 to depth-4 seen stacks all adapted arms land within three to six points of one
another, an order smaller than the gap to the untuned model. Prompting is the exception: the
in-context arm moves accuracy by a few points and is the weakest intervention in the study, which
tells us the failure is not one of answer format.

The strategies separate once the input leaves the training distribution. Measured on the held-out
family and paired by program, pooled training --- the obvious way to spend the data --- is below
every arm assembled from the same rows on all eight models: below the router system by 2.5--4.6
points (significant on all eight) and below the merge by 1.8--3.0 (significant on five). It is also
below an adapter trained on \emph{unobfuscated code alone} on seven of eight. Training on more
transforms made the model worse at a transform it had not seen, which is what memorising a surface
predicts and what an invariance would forbid.

Among the composing strategies, the router system is the strongest forward arm and the most
expensive: it keeps every expert resident and runs a gate at every layer for every token. Its
advantage over the merge is not bought by its two extra experts --- measured against the merge it is
the same size on composites containing neither \texttt{S3} nor \texttt{S4} ($+2.8$ to $+5.3$) as on
those that do ($+2.2$ to $+4.7$), on all eight models.

\begin{takeaway}{RQ2}
Capabilities learned from individual transformations do compose, but how they are combined decides
what survives leaving the training distribution. Pooling the data into one adapter is the weakest
use of it: on the held-out family it is below every arm built from the same rows on 8/8 models, and
below a clean-code-only adapter on 7/8. Composing separately-trained specialists --- by routing or by
merging --- is what carries the capability outside the distribution that produced it.
\end{takeaway}

\subsection{RQ3: Robustness and Generalisation of the Merged Capability}
\label{sec:rq3}
We stress the merged model along three axes beyond its specialists' conditions.

\paragraph{Deeper stacks.} Composition depth does not break it. From depth 2 to depth 4 on seen
transforms the merge holds 110--174\,\% of clean-code accuracy across the panel, and its margin over
pooled training does not narrow with depth.

\paragraph{An unseen obfuscator family.} The merge is above the untuned model on the held-out family
and the stacks containing it on all eight models, by 6.6--17.6 points, significant on every model
where the reference is readable. It is not the \emph{best} arm there --- the router system is ahead
on six of eight --- which bounds the claim: merging carries the capability to an unfamiliar surface,
it does not carry it furthest.

\paragraph{The reversed task.} This is where robustness is decided, because no arm is trained in this
direction. Every single-adapter arm loses accuracy here: pooled training on four of the six models
where it is readable, KL-consistency on five of eight, by as much as 13.2 points. The merge is the
exception --- above the untuned model on seven of eight models by $+3.0$ to $+6.4$, null on the
eighth, and \emph{never significantly below it in any of the three regimes on any model}. Across an
independent second seed on two models the gain reproduces at $+3.56$, $+3.34$, $+3.53$ and $+3.89$,
a spread of half a point.

\paragraph{What the limit is made of.} A control settles why the other arms fail here. Trained with
pooled training's exact recipe but on the \emph{inverse} prompt, an adapter reaches $+10.30$ points
above the untuned model backwards on CodeLlama-7B and $+5.18$ on Llama-3.1-8B --- more than any
forward-trained arm --- so inversion is learnable and the backward losses are caused by forward
training rather than by the task. The transfer is one-way: that backward-trained arm also
\emph{improves} forward accuracy, by $+9.63$ and $+7.19$, while forward training damages the backward
direction. Forward adaptation is narrow in a direction, and it is the direction it was trained on.

\begin{takeaway}{RQ3}
The merged capability survives depth and an unseen obfuscator family, and it is the only arm that
survives the reversed task --- never significantly below the untuned model in any regime on any of
eight models, replicated at a second seed. Its limits are equally clear: it is not the strongest arm
on familiar surfaces or on the unseen family, and the recovery of clean-code accuracy does not
transfer to the untrained direction. A backward-trained control shows why: forward adaptation is
narrow in a direction, not merely narrow.
\end{takeaway}
